```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE,
          fig.width = 5,
          fig.height = 3,
          out.width = "100%",
           message = FALSE,
          fig.align = "center")
options(list(dplyr.summarise.inform = FALSE))
theme_set( theme_classic() )

```

In our first empirically calibrated simulation we simply permuted the treatment assignment labels to create new datasets (with no treatment effect).
In those simulations we found that the estimated standard errors would be systematically too high or too low across permutations.
We wanted to assess whether this was a finite-sample property of the individual datasets, and thus made a new simulation where we generated data according to the distribution of cluster and block sizes, along with a few other descriptive statistics.

In these simulations, we are generating entirely new datasets with each iteration, so are adhering to a superpopulation model rather than a finite population one.



```{r, include=FALSE}


library( clusterRCT )
library( tidyverse )
library( cli )

source( here::here( "fingerprint/load_master_fingerprint_results.R" ) )
```


# Comparing method performances

We next explore how well the methods work, across the scenarios considered.

```{r, include=FALSE}
table( dat$method, useNA="always" )

meth_dat <- dat %>%
  group_by( Collection, UniqueID ) %>%
  nest() %>%
  mutate( data = map( data, summarize_simulation_results, "method" ) ) %>%
  unnest( data ) %>%
  ungroup()

meth_dat  

nrow(studies)
nrow(meth_dat) / nrow(studies)

# Are the estimators SE estimates variously unstable? ----



# Each method estimate for each study
table( meth_dat$method )

meth_dat <- meth_dat %>%
  group_by( UniqueID ) %>%
  mutate( cal = ESEhat / SE,
          rel_SE = SE / median(SE, na.rm=TRUE),
          stab = sdSEhat / median(SE, na.rm=TRUE) ) %>%
  ungroup()
```

\newpage
## Are some methods imperfectly calibrated?

We first examine whether the standard errors are _calibrated_, meaning the average estimated standard error tends to be equal to the true standard error.
This plots across the studies for each estimator.

```{r, warning=FALSE}
ggplot( meth_dat, aes( method, cal )) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  coord_flip() +
  labs( title = "Calibration of SE estimates (E[SE-hat]/SE)",
        subtitle = "Ratio of estimated SE to true SE" ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  geom_hline( yintercept = 1 ) 
```

Some methods do not have estimated standard errors at all for some scenarios.  We drop these missing values, and look at calibration across scenarios where the estimated SEs exist.

Generally, methods are decently calibrated for more scenarios.
The proportion of studies where the estimated standard error is notably less than or greater than the true standard error is shown below:
```{r}
meth_dat %>%
  group_by( method ) %>%
  summarise( n = sum( !is.na( cal ) ),
             below_75 = mean( cal <= 0.75, na.rm=TRUE ),
             above_1.25 = mean( cal >= 1.25, na.rm=TRUE ) ) %>%
  arrange( -below_75 ) %>%
  knitr::kable( digits = 2 )
```

We see that some estimators do have many scenarios where the standard errors are systematically too low (more than 25% too small, give or take some monte carlo uncertainty).

\newpage
## Are some methods more precise?

We next examine whether some methods are, for given scenarios, systematically more or less precise than others.
We, for each scenario, calculate the ratio of the true standard error to the median standard error across methods.
Above 1 means that method is more unstable relative to its peers for that scenario.
Below 1 means it is notably more precise.

```{r, message=FALSE}
ggplot( meth_dat, aes( method, rel_SE )) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  coord_flip() +
  labs( title = "Method true SE to median true SE within study",
        caption = "For TRIAD, 6 ATE estimators are undefined due to degrees of freedom concerns.") +
  theme_minimal() +
  geom_hline( yintercept = 1 ) 
```

One study (TRIAD) is matched pairs, and for this study 6 methods did not even provide a point estimate, meaning there is no standard error.
For those methods, that study is dropped from the above figure.

Here are the performance stats on TRIADScale-up:

```{r}
filter( meth_dat, UniqueID == "TRIADScale-up_rema2" ) %>%
  dplyr::select( -c( UniqueID, Collection, weight, biased ) ) %>%
  knitr::kable( digits = 2 )
```

As another way of tackling the question of which estimators are more or less precise, we can look, within study, at the ratio of largest _true_ SE to smallest _true_ SE.
This is akin to the ratio of estimated SEs (which we did in the paper), but is about differences in true performance.

<!--Below we look at the ratio of true SEs as a function of the median SE.
No strong relationship, and we see outliers with some studies where the choice of estimator apparently matters a great deal.-->

We can make the standard plot of studies, looking at the SE ratio.  But this is the true ratio, not the ratio of the estimated SEs:

```{r}
mm <- meth_dat %>%
  group_by( UniqueID ) %>%
  summarise( medianSE = median(SE),
             trueSEratio = max(SE, na.rm=TRUE) / min(SE, na.rm=TRUE) )
mm <- left_join( mm, studies, by="UniqueID" ) 

#ggplot( mm, aes( medianSE, trueSEratio )) +
#  geom_point()
ggplot( mm, aes( trueSEratio, fill=low_df ) ) +
  geom_dotplot( method="histodot", binwidth=0.1 ) 
```

We are looking at `r nrow(mm)` studies.

We can look at the ranges of true SE by study, to see which studies have greater opportunity for an estimator to be preferred:

```{r}
ggplot( meth_dat, aes( UniqueID, SE )) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  coord_flip() +
  labs( title = "Range of True SEs of methods by study" ) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  theme_minimal()
```


We can look at which studies have the larger differences, by printing out the studies in order of smallest to largest true SE ratio:

```{r}
#mm
mm %>%
  arrange( trueSEratio ) %>%
  dplyr::select( UniqueID, J, Jbar, nbar, num_singletons, trueSEratio ) %>%
  knitr::kable( digits=2 )
```

We can ask what drives these differences, making a tree that predicts which studies have greater instability in the true SE:

```{r}
source( here::here( "create_analysis_tree.R" ) )
create_analysis_tree( mm, "trueSEratio",
                      c("J", "Jbar", "K", "num_singletons",
                        "num_doubletons", "ncv", "Jcv", "tx.cv",
                        "p.tx", "R2.1", "cluster_ICC" ),
                      min_leaves = 4, max_leaves = 7
                      )

if ( FALSE ) {
  mm %>% 
  group_by( tx.cv >= 0.11 ) %>%
  summarise( tx.cv = mean( tx.cv ),
             p.tx = mean( p.tx ),
             mn = mean( trueSEratio, na.rm=TRUE ), 
             n = n())
}
```

This says those studies with larger R2.1 values have greater differences.
This implies that some estimators are taking advantage of the covariates better than others?


We can look at the stats of `jg_crt_12`, but nothing jumps out as being particularly exciting as an explanation.

```{r}
uid = "jg_crt_12"
clusterRCT:::print.clusterRCTstats( filter( studies, UniqueID == uid ) )
```

\newpage
## Are estimated SEs more unstable for some methods?

We next look at whether some methods have more variation in how their estimated standard errors vary across simulation runs for given scenarios.
We compare the standard deviation of SE hat, normalizing by the true median SE (across methods for that scenario) to put everything on the same scale.

```{r}
ggplot( meth_dat, aes( method, stab )) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  coord_flip() +
  labs( title = "sd(SE-hat) / median(SE)" ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

Overall, all the methods have estimated standard errors that seem about the same wiggly, relative to their respective true standard errors.

If we look by study, we see some studies have very reliable stabilities across method.
Other studies have very different stabilities.
```{r}
ggplot( meth_dat, aes( UniqueID, stab )) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  coord_flip() +
  labs( title = "sd(SE-hat) / median(SE)" ) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  theme_minimal()
```


# Looking at true SEs for person vs cluster weighting

We can see if true standard errors were systematically different for some scenarios.
In this plot, we look at how much variation across estimators there were for 

```{r, out.width="100%"}
wts <- meth_dat %>%
  group_by( Collection, UniqueID, weight ) %>%
  summarise( meanSE = median(SE, na.rm=TRUE),
             minSE = min(SE,na.rm=TRUE),
             maxSE = max(SE,na.rm=TRUE),
             sdSE = sd(SE, na.rm=TRUE), .groups = "drop" )

ggplot( wts, aes( UniqueID, meanSE, col=weight ) ) +
 # facet_wrap( ~ Collection, scales="free" ) +
  geom_point( size=3, position=position_dodge(width=0.5), pch="|" ) +
  geom_point( data=meth_dat, aes( y = SE ),
              size = 1,
              alpha=0.5,
              position=position_dodge(width=0.5) ) +
  geom_errorbar( aes( ymin=minSE, ymax=maxSE ),
                 width=0.2, position=position_dodge(width=0.5),
                 alpha=0.5 ) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_log10() +
  theme_minimal()
```

Note the axis is on a log scale so that studies with overall small SEs are not artifically compressed.

We see that some scenarios have very different SEs for some methods, and other scenarios have a very narrow range of SEs.
We do not see systematic differences by estimand--in those studies with different SEs for different methods, the range of SEs within estimand is about the same.
Possible exceptions are jg_crt_6 and jg_crt_17, where some of the the cluster-weighted methods have notibly larger SEs than any of the other methods.


# How different are different studies?

## Which studies tend to have larger differences across methods?

We next look at what kinds of ranges we would see for each study.
For each study we calculate the median range across simulation runs, and then plot the middle 90% interval of ranges observed.
We use a log scale, to again account for how some studies just tend to have larger ranges than other studies.

```{r}
rng <- range_dat %>% 
  mutate( ratioSE = pmin( ratioSE, 5 ) ) %>%
  group_by( Collection, UniqueID ) %>%
  summarise( across( rangeATE:na_SE, list( mn = median, sd=sd,
                                           Q95 = \(x) quantile(x,0.95),
                                           Q05 = \(x) quantile(x,0.05) ) ),
             .groups = "drop" )

ggplot( rng, aes( UniqueID, rangeATE_mn ) ) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_errorbar( aes( ymin=rangeATE_Q05, ymax=rangeATE_Q95 ),
                 width=0, alpha=0.5 ) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs( title = "Mean rangeATE across studies",
        subtitle = "Range of ATEs for each study" ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

The relative ranges of each study seems about the same.
I.e., the variation in range for a given study seems to be mainly dependant on the size of the median range itself.


We can do the same thing for ratio of SE across methods.

```{r}

ggplot( rng, aes( UniqueID, ratioSE_mn ) ) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_errorbar( aes( ymin=ratioSE_Q05, ymax=ratioSE_Q95 ),
                 width=0, alpha=0.5 ) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs( title = "Mean ratioSE across studies",
        subtitle = "Ratio of SEs across permutations for each study" ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

Here it does seem that some studies tend to have much greater variability in the SE ratio across simulation iterations.


```{r, include=FALSE, eval=FALSE}
range_dat$ratioSE[ range_dat$ratioSE > 5 ] = 5
range_dat$UniqueID = fct_reorder( range_dat$UniqueID, 
                                   range_dat$ratioSE, 
                                   .desc = TRUE )

ggplot( range_dat, aes( UniqueID, ratioSE ) ) +
  facet_wrap( ~ Collection, scales="free_y" ) +
  geom_boxplot( fill="grey", outlier.size=0.3 ) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs( title = "ratio of SEs across simulation runs",
        subtitle = "Windorizerd at ratio of 5" ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  scale_y_log10()
```

We see the ratio of SE across methods depends on the average cluster size, but that even for a given cluster size, some studies tend to have much higher ratios than than others:

```{r}
rd = left_join( rng, studies, by="UniqueID" )

ggplot( rd, aes( Jbar, ratioSE_mn ) ) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  geom_smooth( se=FALSE, span=1, method="loess" ) + 
  geom_point()+
  theme_minimal() +
  labs( title = "Typical ratio of SEs across methods",
        subtitle = "Windorizerd at ratio of 5",
        x = "Average cluster size (Jbar)",
        y = "Mean ratio" )
```

We next look more closely at studies where Jbar was less than 4.3:

```{r}
range_dat = left_join( range_dat, studies, by="UniqueID" )
sb <- filter( range_dat, Jbar < 4.3 ) %>%
  mutate( UniqueID = fct_reorder( UniqueID, Jbar, .desc = TRUE ) )

rd %>% 
  arrange( Jbar ) %>%
  filter( Jbar < 4.3 ) %>%
  dplyr::select( UniqueID, J, Jbar, K, ratioSE_mn, rangeATE_mn, na_SE_mn ) %>%
  unique() %>%
  print( n = 15 )

ggplot( sb,
        aes( UniqueID, ratioSE ) ) +
  geom_boxplot( fill="grey", outlier.size=0.3 ) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs( title = "ratio of SEs across simulation runs",
        subtitle = "Studies with Jbar < 4.3; Windorizerd at ratio of 5" ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  scale_y_log10()
```


Some details of two interesting studies:
```{r}
uid = "jg_crt_17"
clusterRCT:::print.clusterRCTstats( filter( studies, UniqueID == uid ) )

clusterRCT:::print.clusterRCTstats( filter( studies, UniqueID == "TennStar_gktreadss" ) )
```



## Which studies generate the highest SE ranges?

We can then explore across the scenarios what characteristics lead to times when some methods truly are more precise than other methods

```{r}


source( here::here( "create_analysis_tree.R" ) )
create_analysis_tree( range_dat, "ratioSE",
                      c("J", "Jbar", "K", "num_singletons",
                        "num_doubletons", "ncv", "Jcv", "tx.cv", "na_SE" ),
                      max_leaves = 7
                      )


triad_id = "TRIADScale-up_rema2"
create_analysis_tree( filter( range_dat, UniqueID != triad_id ), 
                      "rangeATE",
                      c("J", "Jbar", "K", "n", "nbar", "num_singletons",
                        "num_doubletons", "ncv", "Jcv", "tx.cv", "na_SE" ),
                      min_leaves = 10,
                      max_leaves = 10
)
```

# Supplement Stuff




## Sample of Ranges generated

We can sample a five run IDs and look at the ranges we get in a case where we generate data fully at random, fit across our estimators, and calculate the range of estimates:


```{r}
ggplot( sub_dat, aes( rangeATE ) ) +
  facet_grid( weight ~ runID ) +
  geom_dotplot( method="histodot", binwidth = 0.02 ) +
  labs( title = "5 replicates of fingerprint for ATE range" ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

We can do the same for the ratio of standard errors, topcoding the ratio at 5.
```{r}
#summary( sub_dat$ratioSE )
sub_dat$ratioSE[ sub_dat$ratioSE > 5 ] = 5
ggplot( sub_dat, aes( ratioSE ) ) +
  facet_grid( weight ~ runID ) +
  geom_dotplot( method="histodot" ) +
  labs( title = "5 replicates of fingerprint for SE ratio",
        subtitle = "(Ratios windsorized at 5x)" ) +
  theme_minimal()
```
